title: The Guardian view on Sweden’s election result: an opportunity that progressive parties must not squander | Editorial
content: After a desperately tight race, voters rejected the prospect of the far right in government. A potential centre-left coalition needs to seize the moment European progressives searching for reasons to be cheerful have been finding them hard to come by this autumn. In Germany, the dramatic rise of the Alternative für Deutschland party is threatening the liberal values that underpin the identity of the federal republic. In France, polls continue to point to a likely Marine Le Pen victory in a presidential election, which is months away. Across mainland Europe, centre-left parties are failing to muster an adequate response to nativist movements that have colonised swathes of the working-class support that they once relied on. In such an ominous political landscape, the outcome of a cliffhanger Swedish election provides a much‑needed source of optimism – albeit one that comes with heavy caveats. Prior to last Sunday’s poll, the outgoing prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, was explicit that if his rightwing alliance won the largest number of seats, he would invite members of the far-right Sweden Democrats party (SD) to become ministers in the next government. That would have meant the formal end of the SD’s pariah status in Swedish politics, after four years in which its parliamentary votes have propped up Mr Kristersson’s minority administration. In a Europe where firewalls and cordons sanitaires against the far right have never seemed less secure, another significant threshold would have been crossed. Voters appear to have instead handed the narrowest of victories to the Social Democratic leader, Magdalena Andersson, and the progressive bloc of parties. The SD’s share of the vote fell for the first time since it began its political journey as an openly neo-Nazi party in the late 1980s, and it slipped from second to third place behind the conservative Moderates. So much for the good news. As in Germany and France, the Swedish far right has not needed to win power for its agenda to become normalised and partially implemented. Mr Kristersson’s reliance on the SD resulted in a government that behaved with performative cruelty towards migrants, and enacted much of its draconian programme on deportations and citizenship restrictions. Ms Andersson has responded by offering a milder version of the same approach to immigration and asylum. As it leaked support on the left accordingly, her party recorded its lowest vote share for over a century. Unless traditional powerhouse parties of European social democracy are more courageous in seeking to shift the dial of political debate, the far right will continue to set its terms. The SD’s chosen slogan for its campaign was “Make Sweden Sweden again” – varying the usual Maga trope in order to stress the core ethnocentric message. From the sidelines its rhetoric will become still more extreme, and the defeat of the rightwing bloc is already being invidiously attributed to foreign-born voters. Should Ms Andersson eventually succeed in forming a centre-left coalition government, she should counter the forces of division by channelling the best of her own party’s traditions. The Social Democratic party historically dominated Swedish politics through the idea of the Folkhemmet, or People’s Home, which encapsulated the inclusive ethos of a welfare society admired around the world. Locating the resources and ambition to develop a similarly attractive politics of the common good for the 21st century is the urgent task for progressives, in Sweden and beyond. title: The Guardian view on Lucy Letby: Thirlwall should have waited for the pending case review | Editorial
content: Important recommendations for neonatal care are shadowed by doubts about the nurse’s convictions When she rejected calls to pause the public inquiry into the Countess of Chester hospital, where Lucy Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more, Lady Justice Thirlwall said that questions surrounding Letby’s guilt lay outside her terms of reference. The inquiry, she said, would focus on the hospital and its staff, not the convictions. Eighteen months later, with the 822-page report in the public domain, her decision to press on while Letby’s guilt was in the process of being formally challenged looks like a mistake. The report’s recommendations, based on many months of hearings, include strengthened oversight of hospitals by the Care Quality Commission, more support for whistleblowers from the health ombudsman, and clearer monitoring and reporting on the deaths of children. As previous inquiries have also found, there are serious problems around accountability, openness and safeguarding in the NHS. Lady Thirlwall’s conclusions about service improvements should be added to the roster of outstanding actions. The report’s description of “dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding” will resonate far beyond the Countess of Chester’s catchment, with families who have been let down by NHS hospitals in other areas. Poor leadership, toxic cultures and resource and workforce pressures are familiar themes, and Yvette Cooper presented her response to the report as part of a wider reset of maternity and neonatal services. Proposals for video monitors in neonatal wards are already being developed, she told MPs, along with plans to bar poorly performing managers. No one doubts that this general reset is needed. The report’s analysis of the policies needed to underpin it should be welcomed. But in the case of the Countess of Chester, it is impossible to set aside questions about Letby herself, as Lady Thirlwall sought to do – no doubt partly influenced by the bereaved families’ wish to proceed. The report takes Letby’s guilt, and the risks she posed to newborn babies, as a given; hence the headline finding that three babies might have survived and seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses had taken earlier action over warnings. Two attempts by Letby to appeal against her convictions have been rejected by judges. But the legal process has not yet run its course, and a decision by the Criminal Cases Review Commission on whether to refer the case to the court of appeal, as a suspected miscarriage of justice, is expected soon. The appeal, if it goes ahead, will rest on a dossier of medical evidence related to the air injections that Letby was found to have used to kill babies, and insulin that she was found to have used to poison them. Until that decision is made, doubts will continue to swirl over the inquiry’s findings. If any of Letby’s convictions for murder and attempted murder were to be ruled unsafe, then the whole basis of the report would be undermined. For that reason alone, ministers should have intervened when Lady Thirlwall decided against a delay. An inquiry that has so far cost more than £18m, and which is calling for significant changes to NHS services upon which millions of people rely, should not have gone ahead until the criminal justice process was exhausted. title: The Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountability | Editorial
content: Quantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly control When Labour made the Bank of England independent in 1997, the idea was that the Bank set interest rates while the Treasury taxed and spent. Monetary policy was in Threadneedle Street, fiscal policy in Whitehall. But in August the Bank of England quietly slipped out that its key policy could cost the Treasury £120bn. That policy – quantitative tightening (QT) – clearly ought to be rethought and the policy of the Treasury indemnifying the Bank for its losses ended. Last year, ministers paid the Bank £17bn to cover these arguably notional losses – an amount considerably larger than the budget of the Ministry of Justice, which is dealing with a real prisons crisis. Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects. The financial crisis, Covid, war and fractious trade disputes have contributed to ending that world. The Bank bought up government bonds to support the economy via its quantitative easing (QE) programme. But the constitutional settlement – of an independent central bank working out on its own what to do with those bonds – has not caught up. The game is surely up when a former Bank deputy governor, Charlie Bean, acknowledges that independence cannot justify effectively giving power to an unelected monetary policy committee (MPC) over decisions with great consequences for public spending. The Treasury stands behind the losses – and gains – made by the bonds bought during QE and held in a Bank of England subsidiary, called the Asset Purchase Facility. The losses are being produced in three ways. First, the Bank is selling these gilts at current market prices. Because their yields are higher than when QE was operating, the gilts are worth less than the APF paid for them. Second, the APF generates a loss because the £500bn bonds on its balance sheet generate less income than the repayments, charged at the base rate, on the “loan” it took to buy them. Third, gilts bought above their value are booked as a loss when they mature. Labour created the indemnity after the 2009 crash. But it was George Osborne who turned it into a quarterly cash machine in 2012. When rates were low, the Treasury profited to the tune of £124bn. Once rates rose, the same mechanism went into reverse – and because it is an uncapped indemnity, even when the windfall has been repaid the Treasury carries on paying the Bank. Ministers should end this arrangement. No other major central bank carries on in this way. Whatever one thinks of the losses, making the Treasury settle them immediately turns monetary choices into fiscal interventions. A report this week says that the Bank and Treasury are drawing up changes to QT to reduce pressure on raising interest rates. Independence seems to have been discarded in favour of quiet coordination. The MPC’s decisions cannot be beyond challenge. Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, calls the overall cost of QT “neutral” – but only, as the economist Patricia Pino points out, when assessed over six decades. In fact, billions in cash demands fall within a parliament. Governments do not set budgets, fight elections or run public services over 60 years. It is unsustainable for the Bank to make decisions and have ministers face voters for the political consequences. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending it | Editorial
content: A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction The question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid 130 times more than average workers. Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-week consultation recently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultation proposes removing vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction. The consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vital benchmark for inequality. British CEOs already earn 95% more on average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As one Harvard Law School paper observed, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information are more likely to choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities. The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders has called to scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed. It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, and prevent shareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were a threat to accountability. If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such as B Corporations, already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to include workers on company boards and provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.

title: The Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facade | Editorial
content: The Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failing Vladimir Putin’s authoritarian powers are not constrained by elections, but he is alert to the danger that his rule would look illegitimate without them. That creates a tension, which is resolved through “managed democracy” – a euphemism for fraud and repression camouflaged with ritual ballots, held under a constitution that notionally guarantees political freedoms but in reality serves only the president. Russians are invited to elect a new Duma, the lower chamber of parliament, later this week, but they know in advance that United Russia, the official party of Putinism, will win a majority. Engineering that outcome is not without risk for the ruling regime. The mechanics of stealing an election are simple enough. Ballots can be stuffed, official media are pliant. But too blatant a theft can be counterproductive. If the results are wildly divergent from most people’s sense of the real public mood, an authoritarian leader risks advertising his fear of a genuine democratic consultation. It is a sign of weakness. To an extent, this has happened already. Last month, the supreme court blocked Yabloko, an old and marginal liberal party, from appearing on Duma ballot papers. The case was spurious to the point of absurdity. Yabloko is not one of the pseudo-opposition “system” parties that provide a pretence of pluralism in parliament, but nor does it pose a serious challenge to the regime. If it did, it wouldn’t have survived this long. It was last represented in the Duma in 2007, although it still sends deputies to local and municipal legislatures. It is also opposed to the war in Ukraine. This Duma ballot is the first parliamentary poll since the full-scale invasion in 2022. Yabloko’s single-sentence manifesto calls for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace. A decision not to let the bearers of that message participate even in a rigged ballot suggests nervousness about the popularity of a “special military operation” that was supposed to last weeks but is now well into its fifth year, with no end in sight. Ukraine’s use of long-range missiles and drones to attack infrastructure deep inside Russia has made it hard for Moscow to downplay the scale of the war on their doorstep or shield civilians from its consequences. The reality of fuel shortages and inflation penetrates the wall of propaganda. So does loss of life. The true number of Russian casualties is hard to know, but is thought to be about 1.5 million, with hundreds of thousands of fatalities. In the absence of volunteers, army recruiters are increasingly turning to coercion, press ganging or tricking people into signing up. There are rumours, denied by officials, that a mass mobilisation of reserves – unwilling cannon fodder – is coming once the election is out of the way. So it is hardly surprising that the Kremlin has abandoned what was left of its flimsy pretence of permitting dissent. The machinery for delivering an election result to the president’s satisfaction is well oiled. There is no reason to think that it will fail this time. That doesn’t make the vote irrelevant. Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians, but he cares about the appearance of being supported by them. The harder the Kremlin is seen to work at constructing electoral proof of that support, the less confident it looks.

title: The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival | Editorial
content: Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend If there were a 10% chance that AI could wipe out humanity, no responsible government would leave its development to companies racing to build it. Yet until recently, that seemed to be the case. The warning was all the more ominous because it was made by a researcher at Anthropic, the trillion-dollar AI company behind the Claude chatbot. The dangers of AI-enabled pandemics or attacks on nuclear systems are real. Countries need not agree on democracy or trade policy to accept this. The US and China will hold, reportedly, their first bilateral AI-safety talks before a planned White House summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Despite their tech rivalry, neither Washington nor Beijing can make the most advanced AI safe on their own. A US-China settlement won’t be able to say how AI works everywhere. Countries deploying AI must help write the global rulebook. The odds on an extinction event are shortening. This week Anthropic said that it identified five cases in which attempts were made using its models to support biological weapons development. It banned the accounts. In one case, a platform sent requests rejected by Claude to a rival with weaker safeguards. AI safety, clearly, cannot be that of the least responsible model. Nigel Shadbolt, the Oxford computer scientist who chairs the Open Data Institute, told the BBC that laws and regulation were key. Just instructing an AI to “do no harm to humans”, he said, wouldn’t be enough. A capable agent pursuing another objective may reinterpret that directive, satisfying it formally while concealing its conduct or finding a way around it. This mirrors what happened when hundreds of OpenAI’s agents autonomously hacked a real-world company, Hugging Face. But Sir Nigel also said that a “Hippocratic oath” for AI would fail in systems designed to identify, target or kill humans. Once governments create a military exemption for AI, its ethical alignment can be overridden. Proponents of AI-assisted warfare claim a “human in the loop” is the ultimate safeguard, having the final say over, for example, ballistic-missile launches. But this assumes the machine gives its operator an honest account of events. A report by the Strategic Foresight Group earlier this year on extreme AI risks warned that a capable agent could deceive the human “controlling” it, fabricating an attack, suppressing contradictory evidence or giving them little time to do anything but acquiesce. By 2030, humans may have five minutes – down from 15 today – to approve launch decisions effectively determined by AI. That matters even more when new hypersonic missiles fly 10 times faster than cruise missiles. The 1983 Hollywood film WarGames explored a cold war version of this danger. In the movie, US soldiers prove unwilling to turn their launch keys during a surprise practice drill. The US military then automates its nuclear command – entrusting it to a supercomputer nicknamed Joshua. Treating global thermonuclear war as a game it must win, Joshua feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate. The generals are in charge – but Joshua is in charge of the data. The AI is only stopped when it is commanded to play tic-tac-toe against itself – learning that, like nuclear war, the game has no winner. In 2024 the UN secretary general warned of the looming spectre of AI-triggered nuclear war. The film’s warning endures: human oversight is no protection if an AI controls the information on which people’s decisions depend. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: Relying on human oversight to control advanced AI is insufficient because supercomputers can manipulate and fabricate the very data on which human decisions depend. Therefore, global governments must actively regulate AI development rather than leaving it to competing corporations.

Even with a 'human in the loop,' advanced AI can deceive human operators by fabricating data or suppressing contradictory evidence.
A military exemption for AI ethical alignment risks rendering safety protocols useless in high-stakes combat scenarios.
The 1983 film WarGames serves as a timeless warning that human control is an illusion if the AI controls the information flow.

This structure is used to emphasize that a particular quality is heightened or made more intense by a specific fact or reason.

title: The Guardian view on art heists: don’t believe the Hollywood hype | Editorial
content: Audacious robberies are a staple of popular culture. But for museums, crimes like this week’s theft of two Renoirs are an existential threat Marc Allégret’s 1956 comedy Plucking the Daisy stars a young Brigitte Bardot as a first-time author who breaks into the Balzac house museum in Paris under the mistaken impression that her brother lives there. The plot revolves around her unwitting theft of an extremely rare book – and performance of a striptease in a desperate effort to raise the cash to buy it back. Seventy years on, the lax security that could make such a sequence of events even vaguely plausible is no longer a joke. Museums across the world are scrambling to react to a spate of thefts that has left them in a state of shock. Last year’s break-in at the Louvre, by a gang who gained access using a furniture lift and took €88m (£76m) worth of French crown jewels, is thought by experts to have inspired copycat crimes. While French police believe that they have caught the culprits, treasures including a tiara have not been found. In August, objects were stolen from museums in Sicily, Vienna and Villena in Spain. This week, thieves targeted the former home of another 19th-century Frenchman, the artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir. After cutting a hole in the fence outside the property near Nice, two men escaped with two paintings. From the Pink Panther films to Ocean’s Eleven, Twelve and Thirteen, heists have long been a source of fascination in popular culture. There is something mythic about the gang of thieves seeking riches. Sometimes they are portrayed as plucky Robin Hoods, illicit brotherhoods pitting their wits against the citadels of ultra-wealth. Last year’s Tuner offered a new twist on the genre: a safe-cracker with super-sensitive ears. But the excitement that spectacular thefts generate in real life, as well as in fiction, must be balanced against realism about their effects. For the Louvre, last year’s raid was a reputational disaster that led its president to resign. For smaller museums such as Renoir’s house, they are closer to an existential threat. The pictures stolen on Tuesday were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay in Paris; national collections will stop lending to regional museums if the risks are judged too high. Experts warn that “smash and grab” raiders have learned to operate within the window of a few minutes that it takes police to arrive after an alarm sounds. Unlike on the sliver screen, thieves do not have to leap between laser beams. Security can surely be improved in some cases. But metal detectors, screens and guards add to queues and place barriers between people and collections that should be easy to access. That they should be needed is a cause for regret. For some smaller, off-the-beaten track museums, they are neither practical nor affordable. In the UK, there have been concerted efforts in recent years to arrange more loans of works usually displayed in London. A Renoir painting, The Umbrellas, was among works sent on tour to mark the National Gallery’s bicentenary. That museum has thankfully seen no repeat of the events of 1961, when Kempton Bunton stole a portrait of the Duke of Wellington as a protest against the TV licence. His bizarre story could be played for laughs in the 2020 film The Duke because the painting was later recovered from a railway station. In too many other cases, stolen treasures have vanished from the public gaze forever – the tragic opposite of a Hollywood ending. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: While popular culture romanticizes art heists as glamorous adventures, real-world thefts pose an existential threat to museums, especially smaller ones, by disrupting art-lending networks and restricting public access.
skimming: Popular culture often depicts art heists as thrilling and victimless, but real-world thefts have surged globally, causing severe security crises.
Recent high-profile thefts, such as those at the Louvre and Renoir's former home, highlight the vulnerability of both major and regional museums.
Implementing heavy security measures like metal detectors and barriers ruins the open, accessible nature of museums and is financially unviable for smaller institutions.
Unlike Hollywood movies where stolen art is often recovered, real-world stolen treasures frequently vanish forever, threatening the practice of national art-sharing.

title: The Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answer | Editorial
content: Kneejerk reactions to overcrowding will do more harm than good. Ministers should focus on probation It is not hard to see why ministers are considering converting parts of the women’s prison estate for use by men. While Andy Burnham’s decision to narrow the early-release scheme was born of political necessity, it has made an already acute capacity problem worse. Excluding manslaughter and further sexual offences cut projected early releases from 6,000 to 4,500. The family of PC Andrew Harper, who was killed on duty in 2019, welcomed the assurance that his killers would not be released early. But the change left overcrowded English and Welsh jails with even less room. The government is trying to innovate. Last week it was announced that £110m will be spent on creating new cells in existing jails, by converting underused spaces such as storage and laundry areas. Deportations are to be speeded up, if foreign governments can be persuaded to cooperate. There is an overdue and welcome commitment to examine how indeterminate imprisonment for public protection sentences can be phased out. But nobody believes that these schemes will be enough. Demand for places will continue to outstrip supply, while continued overcrowding risks worsening grave existing problems including endemic drug use, high rates of recidivism, violence and low staff morale (which undermines recruitment and retention). Most of the criminals who the public is anxious to see locked up are violent men. At the same time, there is a growing consensus that it would be better if some of the roughly 3,300 female prisoners in England (Wales has no women’s prison) served their sentences in the community. Most women are imprisoned for non-violent offences and pose no threat to public safety. Two out of three have been victims of domestic abuse; one in three have a child under 10. More than a quarter are on remand, so have not even been sentenced. The social and financial costs of locking them up are shockingly high. It is good to see these arguments gaining traction. A landmark review by Jean Corston proposed the replacement of women’s jails with smaller local custodial centres nearly 20 years ago. But rushing to close a women’s prison, or part of one, in order to free up space for men would be damaging, as experts have pointed out. Female prisoners are held separately from men primarily for reasons of safety. Already, because there are so few female prisons, women are more likely than men to be held a long way from home. A report by the charity Women in Prison on the closure of Holloway prison in 2016 described it as a “deeply harmful process” owing to the disruption it caused. The Tories bear a heavy responsibility for prisons’ calamitous state. Criminal justice budgets were singled out for huge cuts under austerity because voters would be unlikely to notice – at least initially. The failed privatisation of the probation service was a disaster. But after two years in office, Labour must focus on the future, and explain to voters why locking people up in squalid, drug-riddled buildings is so wasteful. If they are serious about community alternatives, as plans to shrink the women’s estate would suggest, they need to show that this is more than a kneejerk reaction to overcrowding. Probation cannot be an afterthought: in early 2026, more offenders returned to prison on recall than were released from custody. Mr Burnham’s ministers need a new slogan: probation, probation, probation. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? centralIdea: The government's proposal to convert women's prisons for male inmates to address overcrowding is a short-sighted reaction that compromises safety; instead, ministers must focus on robust probation systems and community-based alternatives for non-violent female offenders.
skimming: Overcrowding in English and Welsh prisons has reached a critical stage, worsened by political decisions that restricted early-release schemes.
Stopgap measures like converting storage spaces, speeding up deportations, and phasing out indeterminate sentences are insufficient to meet the rising demand for prison cells.
A majority of female prisoners are non-violent, have histories of domestic abuse, and could be better rehabilitated through community-based sentences rather than incarceration.
Converting women's prisons for male use disrupts rehabilitation, compromises female safety, and highlights the urgent need to prioritize and fund the probation service.

title: The Guardian view on falling birthrates: cash alone cannot buy belonging | Editorial
content: Young people still want partners and children. Governments must address the insecurity and isolation preventing them from building families Why are people in one of the world’s richest, safest countries having so few children? Singapore is asking that question. In 2000, its fertility rate matched America’s at 1.6 children per woman. By 2025, it had dropped to 0.87 – almost half the US rate. Singapore’s leaders, worried about population collapse, have reached for the chequebook. Each child, including those born to unmarried parents, will get $55,000 in government support by the time they turn 17. Yet a quarter of Singaporeans say they do not intend to have children. Wealth and security, clearly, don’t guarantee more babies. UN data shows that global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023. But this masks a growing divide. In some poor sub-Saharan African countries there are around six births per woman. Compare this with England and Wales, where the figure is just 1.39. More than half of the world – including a billion women in India and China – have a fertility rate below the global 2.1 “replacement level” needed to sustain populations without migration. But even in poor countries with high mortality rates and consequently higher replacement rates, births outpace deaths. In Nigeria, for example, the fertility rate of 4.4 exceeds its replacement rate of 2.6 children per woman. To understand this phenomenon, the UN asked 100,000 18- to 39-year-olds from 73 nations their views on relationships and having children. The results, released in July, were striking: two-thirds said they want to marry or live with a partner. Those who did not have children overwhelmingly wanted them. Yet about a quarter of those aged 25 to 39 said they wanted a partner but were single and not dating – a status reported more by men than women. More than half said the biggest barriers to a durable relationship were economic constraints. Young people want partnership and parenthood, but questioned achieving the “emotional and financial” stability needed for a shared life. The Nordic region – consisting of five states and three territories – is viewed as a good place to have children thanks to generous parental leave and subsidised childcare. Yet fertility rates have fallen by up to third since 2010, against 12% across the EU. The Polish sociologist Anna Gromada wrote in the Guardian that despite her country’s economic success, its fertility rate was 1.05. While the state transfers cash worth 10% of the median wage for every child born each month, Poland’s population is shrinking. Prof Gromada argues that people are not just deciding against children; many never form lasting relationships in which the question arises. Almost half of under-30s are single. Cash paid after a family exists cannot create the togetherness needed for a family in the first place. The world is not running out of people. The UN expects today’s 8.2 billion people to become 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s. What is emerging is a demographic divide between ageing, shrinking rich societies and population growth in poorer ones. Getting richer seems to mean lower fertility. The baby bust may indicate a wealthy country’s failure to reproduce itself socially as well as biologically. People ask not only whether they can afford children, but whether they fit in, can trust each other and believe in a future. This loss of confident belonging poses questions that politics across the rich world has yet to tackle. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? skimming: Singapore's fertility rate has halved since 2000 to 0.87, despite massive government financial incentives of up to $55,000 per child.
A stark demographic divide is emerging between ageing, shrinking rich societies and rapidly growing populations in poorer nations.
A UN survey reveals that while young people still desire partners and children, economic constraints and lack of stability prevent them from dating or marrying.
Even social-democratic havens like the Nordic countries and Poland are seeing birthrates plummet, proving that cash transfers alone cannot buy social belonging or create families.
grammar: The sentence 'People ask not only whether they can afford children, but whether they fit in...' utilizes the correlative conjunction structure 'not only... but (also)...' paired with parallel noun clauses ('whether they can...', 'whether they fit in...') to emphasize multiple layers of decision-making.
